course.title: AP Precalculus

topic.title: The Tangent Function
topic.summary: The tangent function as the slope of the terminal ray, its period of π, its vertical asymptotes, its increasing and changing concavity between asymptotes, and its additive and multiplicative transformations.

questions.prompt: What is the period of the tangent function, f(θ) = tan θ?
questions.explanation: The slope of the terminal ray repeats every one-half revolution, so the period of tangent is π.
choiceExplanations: 2π is the period of sine and cosine; tangent repeats sooner.
π/2 is the distance from a zero to the next asymptote.
Half a revolution gives the same slope.
1/π is the frequency of tangent, not its period.
questions.distinguisher: Rays half a turn apart lie on the same line, so they have the same slope.

questions.prompt: Where does the graph of y = tan θ have vertical asymptotes? (k represents any integer.)
questions.explanation: Tangent has periodic asymptotic behavior at θ = π/2 + kπ, because cos θ = 0 at those values.
choiceExplanations: At θ = kπ, sin θ = 0, so these are the zeros of tangent.
This misses the asymptotes at 3π/2, −π/2, and every other one.
At π/4 + kπ, tan θ = 1.
cos θ = 0 at every odd multiple of π/2.
questions.distinguisher: Zeros come from sin θ = 0; asymptotes come from cos θ = 0.

questions.prompt: What is the value of tan(5π/4)?
questions.explanation: The terminal ray of 5π/4 lies on the line y = x in Quadrant III, so its slope is 1. Also (−√2/2)/(−√2/2) = 1.
choiceExplanations: Both sine and cosine are negative in Quadrant III, so their ratio is positive.
The terminal ray has slope 1.
√2/2 is the size of the sine and cosine, not their ratio.
cos(5π/4) ≠ 0, so the tangent is defined.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the graph of y = tan θ on the interval −π/2 < θ < π/2?
choices: Increasing, concave up and then concave down
Increasing, concave down and then concave up
Decreasing, concave down and then concave up
questions.explanation: Between consecutive asymptotes the tangent function increases, and its graph changes from concave down to concave up, at the point of inflection (0, 0).
choiceExplanations: This has the order of concavity reversed.
Concave down for θ < 0 and concave up for θ > 0.
Tangent increases between asymptotes unless it is reflected.
The graph is concave down to the left of θ = 0.
questions.distinguisher: Rising out of −∞ means concave down first.

questions.prompt: What is the period of f(θ) = 3 tan(2θ) − 1?
questions.explanation: The period of a tan(b(θ + c)) + d is |1/b|π = (1/2)π = π/2.
choiceExplanations: π = 2π/2 uses the sine rule; tangent's period starts at π, not 2π.
|1/b|π with b = 2.
2π multiplies by b instead of dividing.
a = 3 stretches the graph vertically; it does not change the period.
questions.distinguisher: Divide π, not 2π, by |b| for tangent.

questions.prompt: Where does the graph of g(θ) = tan(θ − π/4) have vertical asymptotes? (k represents any integer.)
questions.explanation: The graph is y = tan θ shifted π/4 units to the right, so each asymptote moves from π/2 + kπ to 3π/4 + kπ.
choiceExplanations: At θ = π/4 + kπ, the input θ − π/4 is kπ, so these are the zeros of g.
These are the asymptotes of y = tan θ before the shift.
θ − π/4 = π/2 + kπ gives θ = 3π/4 + kπ.
This shifts the asymptotes π/4 to the left instead of to the right.
questions.distinguisher: θ − π/4 shifts right; solve θ − π/4 = π/2 + kπ.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true about the graph of f(θ) = −2 tan θ?
choices: It is increasing between consecutive asymptotes.
It is decreasing between consecutive asymptotes.
questions.explanation: a = −2 < 0 reflects the graph of y = tan θ over the x-axis, so f decreases between consecutive asymptotes.
choiceExplanations: y = tan θ increases; the reflection reverses that.
Tangent graphs are unbounded, so they have no amplitude; 2 is the dilation factor.
Vertical dilations do not change the period, which is still π.
The reflection over the x-axis turns increasing into decreasing.
questions.distinguisher: A negative a reflects the graph; it does not create an amplitude.

questions.prompt: The points of inflection of the graph of y = tan θ + 3 all lie on which line?
questions.explanation: Adding 3 translates the graph and the line containing its points of inflection up 3 units, from y = 0 to y = 3.
choiceExplanations: y = 0 contains the inflection points of y = tan θ before the translation.
The inflection points (kπ, 3) all lie on y = 3.
A vertical translation does not move points onto a vertical line.
π is the period, which describes horizontal spacing.
questions.distinguisher: d moves the line through the inflection points.

questions.prompt: For an angle θ, sin θ = −3/5 and cos θ = 4/5. What is the value of tan θ?
choiceExplanations: Sine divided by cosine.
−4/3 is cosine divided by sine, upside down.
Sine is negative and cosine is positive, so the ratio is negative.
−3/5 is sin θ itself.

questions.prompt: A student claims that tan θ can never be greater than 1, because sin θ and cos θ are both between −1 and 1. Which of the following is the best response?
choices: The student is correct, because a ratio of two numbers between −1 and 1 is between −1 and 1.
The student is incorrect, because tan θ = cos θ/sin θ.
The student is correct, because the maximum value of tan θ is tan(π/4) = 1.
The student is incorrect, because as cos θ approaches 0, the ratio sin θ/cos θ grows without bound.
questions.explanation: Dividing by a number close to 0 gives a large result. Near θ = π/2, sin θ is close to 1 and cos θ is close to 0, so tan θ increases without bound. For example, tan(1.5) ≈ 14.1.
choiceExplanations: Dividing by a small number, such as 0.1, gives a quotient larger than 1.
tan θ = sin θ/cos θ, not the other way around.
tan θ keeps increasing past π/4 on the way to the asymptote at π/2.
Near the asymptotes, tan θ is unbounded.
questions.distinguisher: A small denominator makes a large quotient.
